01.note: A woman who bled whenever she had intercourse came to Shmuel. He told Rav Dimi bar Yosef to go and frighten her, but when he did, nothing fell from her. Shmuel said she was filled with blood that falls out during intercourse, and that such a woman has no cure. Another woman told Rabbi Yohanan that every time she came up from the ritual bath she saw blood. He suggested the gossip of the women of her town had reached her, and told her to immerse in the river and be with her husband on its bank; others report he told her to tell her friends, so they would turn kind or pray for her. Rav Yosef said such a case happened in Pumbedita, and the woman was cured.
01.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had a bleeding woman frightened and a mass of blood fell from her, curing her. These cases follow as companions: the same remedy failing under Shmuel, and a different kind of bleeding treated by Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage to whom a woman who bled during intercourse came for help.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: Sent by Shmuel to frighten the woman.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage consulted by a woman who saw blood each time she left the ritual bath.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who reports a similar case in Pumbedita in which the woman was cured.

terms.meaning: A pool in which a woman immerses after her menstrual period ends; only after immersing may she resume relations with her husband.
A commandment; here, the required immersion that makes a woman permitted to her husband again.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the core legal text the Gemara discusses.
A town in Babylonia, named here as the place of a similar case.

02.note: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi immersed herself in a ritual bath. When she came up, a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required her to immerse again.
02.why: The Gemara is discussing which parts of the body must be clean and free of anything blocking the water before immersion, even if the water need not reach them. The Gemara draws from this case that, for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, nothing foreign may be even inside the mouth.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident, as quoted by Ravin bar Rav Adda.

people.name: Ravin bar Rav Adda
people.about: Passes on Rabbi Yitzhak's report of the incident.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose maidservant immersed; he ruled she must immerse again.

terms.meaning: Dipping the whole body in a ritual bath to become ritually pure; nothing may come between the body and the water.
Blocking: an object between the body and the water that can make an immersion invalid.

03.note: Rav Adda recalled an incident to Rav Hinnana from Sura. The wife of Abba Mari, the Exilarch, quarreled with her husband and would not go to immerse so as to become permitted to him. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak went to calm her, and she said: what can be done now? Come back tomorrow. He understood she meant she had not washed her hair in daylight, and answered: are you lacking kettles, buckets or servants?
03.why: The Sages disagree whether a woman may wash her hair at night and immerse that same night; Rav Hinnana permits it. The Gemara reads Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's reply as showing he too holds that washing and immersing the same night is permitted.

people.name: Rav Adda
people.about: Recalls this incident to Rav Hinnana from Sura.

people.name: Rav Ḥinnana from Sura
people.about: The Sage who permits washing the hair and immersing on the same night.

people.name: Abba Mari
people.about: The Exilarch, whose wife quarreled with him.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Went to calm the Exilarch's wife and persuade her to immerse.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful official.
After her period a wife must immerse in a ritual bath, having first washed and combed her hair, before relations with her husband may resume.

04.note: In the town of Galahi, the rule was that a man with one ox shepherded the town's herd for one day, and a man with no ox shepherded it for two. An orphan, the son of a widow, who had no oxen, was given the townspeople's oxen to shepherd, and he went and slaughtered them all. He told them that whoever had an ox should take one hide and whoever had none should take two. When they asked what he meant, he said the end of the law is like its beginning: if the man with no ox gets more at the start, he gets more at the end too.
04.why: Rava has just mocked a ruling that a woman who saw no blood needs more immersions than one who did, calling it like the law of Galahi, where the man with no ox shepherds longer. The Gemara then tells this tale of Galahi.

people.name: orphan, the son of a widow
people.about: A boy with no oxen, given the town's oxen to shepherd, who slaughtered them.

terms.meaning: A place the Gemara says judged in the manner of Sodom, with unfair rules like this one.
